topicName: Cluster Gossip Protocol, Meet Messages, and Failover Detection
content: [{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Cluster Gossip Protocol, Meet Messages, and Failover Detection in Redis"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Redis Cluster provides a decentralized way to run a Redis installation where data is automatically sharded across multiple nodes. To maintain topology and cluster state without a centralized coordinator, Redis utilizes an asynchronous Gossip Protocol. This tutorial explores how Redis nodes discover each other, exchange state via Meet messages, and detect node failures for automatic failover."},{"order":3,"type":"heading","text":"1. The Redis Gossip Protocol Basics"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"Every Redis Cluster node maintains a TCP connection with every other node in the cluster, forming a full mesh network. However, nodes do not continuously broadcast state to everyone. Instead, they run a gossip protocol where nodes periodically exchange packets to spread information about the cluster configuration and the health of other nodes."},{"order":5,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Cluster Bus: Nodes communicate using a binary protocol over a dedicated port, which is typically the client port plus 10000 (e.g., port 16379 for a node running on 6379)."},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Periodic Exchange: Every second, a node randomly selects a few nodes and sends ping packets to the ones it has communicated with the least recently, ensuring overall cluster convergence."},{"order":7,"type":"heading","text":"2. Meet Messages and Node Discovery"},{"order":8,"type":"paragraph","text":"When you add a new node to an existing Redis Cluster, it is initially isolated. It does not know about the other nodes until it receives a 'MEET' message. A MEET message forces the receiving node to accept the sender as part of the cluster and add it to its node table."},{"order":9,"type":"code","text":"CLUSTER MEET <ip> <port>"},{"order":10,"type":"paragraph","text":"Executing the command above on an existing node causes it to send a MEET packet to the target IP and port. Once received, the target node responds with a PONG packet, and both nodes begin regular gossip exchanges. Through the gossip mechanism, the new node's existence rapidly propagates to all other nodes in the full mesh."},{"order":11,"type":"heading","text":"3. Failover Detection: PFAIL and FAIL States"},{"order":12,"type":"paragraph","text":"Redis uses a two-phase failure detection mechanism to distinguish between transient network issues and actual node crashes. This relies on local timeouts and cluster-wide consensus."},{"order":13,"type":"bullet_point","text":"PFAIL (Possible Fail): If a node fails to respond to a ping packet within the cluster-node-timeout limit, it is marked locally as PFAIL. This is a subjective state."},{"order":14,"type":"bullet_point","text":"FAIL (Fail): A node transitions from PFAIL to FAIL when a quorum of master nodes agrees that the node is unresponsive. Gossip messages carry flags about nodes in PFAIL, allowing other nodes to aggregate failure reports."},{"order":15,"type":"paragraph","text":"Once a node reaches the FAIL state, a broadcast is sent to all cluster nodes, forcing everyone to mark the node as dead and trigger a failover if the dead node was a master."},{"order":16,"type":"heading","text":"4. Configuring Cluster Timeouts"},{"order":17,"type":"paragraph","text":"The responsiveness of the gossip protocol and failover detection is heavily governed by the cluster-node-timeout configuration directive in your redis.conf file."},{"order":18,"type":"code","text":"cluster-node-timeout 15000"},{"order":19,"type":"paragraph","text":"In this example, the timeout is set to 15 seconds. If a node is unreachable for more than 7.5 seconds (half the timeout value), peers will flag it as PFAIL. Tuning this value requires balancing fast failover detection against false positives caused by temporary network congestion."}]
